editorial_policy: Curated factual summaries verified against linked WHO and CPCB pages, not a live scraped corpus; review when sources change.

sources.title: WHO global air quality guidelines
sources.fact: The WHO 2021 air quality guideline for PM2.5 is 5 micrograms per cubic metre as an annual average and 15 micrograms per cubic metre as a 24-hour average. These reference concentrations must be compared with measurements over the same averaging periods, not with a single instantaneous sensor reading.

sources.title: WHO global air quality guidelines
sources.fact: WHO 2021 recommends a PM10 annual average of 15 micrograms per cubic metre and a 24-hour average of 45 micrograms per cubic metre. A momentary PM10 value is not a valid direct test of either averaging-time guideline.

sources.title: WHO global air quality guidelines
sources.fact: WHO 2021 recommends an annual mean nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentration of 10 micrograms per cubic metre and a 24-hour mean of 25 micrograms per cubic metre. These are health-based concentration guidelines, not AQI values.

sources.title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines Q&A
sources.fact: Fine particles such as PM2.5 can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. WHO links air pollution with respiratory and cardiovascular harm. These population-level findings do not diagnose any individual or predict an individual's risk from a single reading.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO lists children, pregnant people, older adults, outdoor workers and people with existing heart or lung disease among groups needing particular care about air-pollution exposure.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: During high pollution, sensitive people may need to reduce strenuous outdoor activity or change its time or location. A forecast cannot guarantee a safe hour; physical activity also has benefits.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: Being indoors may reduce outdoor exposure, but cooking, smoking, incense, building ventilation and outdoor infiltration also affect indoor air. Outdoor AQI cannot measure indoor pollutant levels.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: Portable air filters can lower particles in some settings, but real-world health outcomes and effectiveness vary. Maintenance, cost and building conditions matter; fixed benefits cannot be promised.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: Certified, well-fitted and correctly used particulate respirators can reduce particle inhalation. Fit varies; no mask guarantees safety. People with medical conditions may need professional advice.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO prioritizes reducing pollution at its sources. Logging personal habits cannot itself establish a specific reduction in CO2 emissions, citywide AQI or health problems.

sources.title: National Air Quality Index
sources.fact: India's CPCB National AQI categories are Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400), and Severe (401–500). These are CPCB AQI bands, not US AQI categories; the two index scales cannot be directly compared.

sources.title: National Air Quality Index
sources.fact: The CPCB describes increasing potential breathing discomfort as India's National AQI rises; its Severe category may affect healthy people and seriously affect people with existing diseases. Official local advisories and conditions should guide decisions.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO cautions that countries calculate AQIs differently. Their numeric indices are not directly comparable. Display pollutant units and averaging periods as well as the relevant local index.
